name: Methylphenidate
addictionPotential: Moderately addictive with a high potential for abuse
toxicities: DailyMed warns that misuse and abuse can cause overdose and death, with risk increased at higher doses or by unapproved routes. Reported misuse effects include tachycardia, increased blood pressure, sweating, restlessness, insomnia, tremor, vomiting, anxiety, psychosis, hostility, aggression, and suicidal or homicidal thoughts.

Overdose can cause tachyarrhythmias, hypertension or hypotension, vasospasm, myocardial infarction, agitation, confusion, hallucinations, serotonin syndrome, seizures, stroke, coma, life-threatening hyperthermia, and rhabdomyolysis.
Therapeutic use also carries warnings for serious cardiac disease, increased blood pressure and heart rate, and new or worsened psychotic or manic symptoms.
summary: A psychostimulant commonly used in the treatment of ADHD, narcolepsy and obesity, particularly in the EU instead of Adderall. Methylphenidate is also a 5HT1A receptor agonist. Sometimes prescribed off-label to help the withdrawals from cocaine and other stimulants.
effectsSummary: Taking methylphenidate increases the concentration of the nerve messengers dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin in the brain. When prescribed for ADHD, the drug is supposed to act as a filter for incoming stimuli and alleviate symptoms such as distractibility, attention deficit disorder, disorganisation and impulsivity. However, due to its stimulating, energising and drive-enhancing properties, methylphenidate is also used as a party drug or to increase performance. Due to the increased release of dopamine, similar effects occur as with the use of cocaine.
generalRisks: The label is specifically for methylphenidate extended-release capsules (oral, Schedule II; revised 2025-09). It carries a boxed warning for abuse, misuse, addiction, overdose, and death; it warns about serious cardiac disease, increased blood pressure/heart rate, psychiatric reactions, seizures and overdose. Do not generalize the ER product dosing directions to other formulations.
longtermRisks: It is assumed that no dependence develops with therapeutic use of Ritalin. When abusing higher doses over a longer period of time, psychological dependence may develop. With abrupt discontinuation, withdrawal symptoms such as lethargy, apathy, depression and paranoia may occur.
saferUse: Do not use another person's prescription or alter an extended-release product; the cited label warns that misuse, including taking it in a way that is not approved, can cause overdose and death.

The label reports near-complete early release in an in-vitro test at 40% alcohol concentration. Ask a prescriber or pharmacist about alcohol exposure, and do not assume the product release profile is unaffected.
Chest pain, fainting, severe agitation, hallucinations, seizure, very high temperature, or suspected overdose requires urgent medical care.
metabolism: Primarily hydrolyzed by de-esterification to ritalinic acid (PPAA), which has little or no activity. Metabolites account for most urinary elimination.
dosageRemark: The label is for oral extended-release capsules indicated for ADHD in children 6–12; its prescription regimen is not recreational dose guidance. Existing route-specific recreational thresholds were not changed.
